name: LG C5 OLED evo TV
amazonQuery: LG 65 inch OLED evo C5 4K TV
summary: The default OLED for most home theaters: perfect blacks, Dolby Vision, four HDMI 2.1 ports at 144 Hz and sizes from 42" to 83".
verdict:
The LG C5 OLED evo is the TV we would point most home theater buyers to first. Every pixel makes its own light, so blacks are truly black and there is no blooming around subtitles. It supports **Dolby Vision, HDR10 and HLG**, runs **webOS 25**, and all **four HDMI ports are HDMI 2.1** with 4K at up to **144 Hz** (see [HDMI 2.1](/glossary/hdmi-2-1/)).

Size it for your seat. A 65" screen is 56.7" wide, so a 40-degree viewing angle puts you about **6.5 ft** away and a 30-degree angle about **8.8 ft**. At 77" (67.1" wide), those figures become about 7.7 ft and 10.4 ft. Run your room through our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/). If you sit 10 ft or more from the screen, the 77" is the better buy.

Four HDMI 2.1 ports matter in a theater: one goes to a soundbar or receiver over **eARC** (see [eARC](/glossary/earc/)), leaving three full-bandwidth inputs for a console, a PC and a streamer. At 144 Hz, each frame lasts about 6.9 ms, which helps PC gaming feel smooth. The trade-off is brightness: in a sunny room, the [Samsung S95F OLED TV](/gear/samsung-s95f/) gets noticeably brighter, LG's newer [LG C6 OLED evo TV](/gear/lg-c6-oled/) adds a Brightness Booster, and Mini LED sets like the [TCL QM8L SQD-Mini LED TV](/gear/tcl-qm8l/) go brighter still. For a dim or dark room, the C5 is a top pick in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/).

faqs.q: What size LG C5 should I buy for my room?
faqs.a: Work from your seating distance. At about 6.5 to 8.8 feet, a 65-inch C5 fills a 30 to 40-degree field of view. At about 7.7 to 10.4 feet, the 77-inch does. Most people who sit around 9 to 10 feet away end up happier with the larger size.

faqs.q: Is the LG C5 good for gaming?
faqs.a: Yes. All four HDMI ports support HDMI 2.1 with 4K at up to 144 Hz, plus variable refresh rate. Combined with OLED pixel response, it is one of the best gaming TVs at its price.

name: LG C6 OLED evo TV
amazonQuery: LG 65 inch OLED evo C6 4K TV 2026
summary: LG's 2026 C-series OLED: self-lit pixels, a Brightness Booster driven by the a11 AI Processor Gen3, refresh up to 165 Hz with G-Sync and FreeSync Premium, plus Dolby Vision and Filmmaker Mode.
verdict:
The LG C6 OLED evo is LG's 2026 C-series and takes the G5's place on our list as the newest LG OLED. Each of its **8.3 million pixels** makes its own light, so blacks are truly black, with no blooming around subtitles. New for this generation is a **Brightness Booster** driven by the **a11 AI Processor Gen3**, which LG says delivers 5.6x the AI processing of its a9 Gen8 chip. You also get **Dolby Vision**, **Dolby Atmos**, **Filmmaker Mode** with Ambient Light Technology, and **webOS** with Google Gemini.

Gamers get a lot: refresh up to **165 Hz** with VRR, **NVIDIA G-Sync** and **AMD FreeSync Premium**, and a 0.1 ms response time. At 165 Hz each frame lasts about **6.1 ms**, against 8.3 ms at 120 Hz.

Size it for your seat. The 65" model is **56.7" wide**. A 40-degree viewing angle puts you about **6.5 ft** away and a 30-degree angle about **8.8 ft**; if your sofa is 10 ft or more back, look at a bigger screen or a projector. Check your room with our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/). The stand is 9.1" deep, so measure your media unit too.

LG's listing gives no peak-brightness figure, so do not expect it to match Mini LED sets such as the [TCL QM8L SQD-Mini LED TV](/gear/tcl-qm8l/) in a sunny room; the matte [Samsung S95F OLED TV](/gear/samsung-s95f/) is the OLED for bright spaces. In a dim or dark theater, the C6 is a top pick in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/), and last year's [LG C5 OLED evo TV](/gear/lg-c5-oled/) is worth a look if you find it for less.

name: Samsung S90F OLED TV
summary: A strong-value OLED with up to 144 Hz gaming, four HDMI 2.1 ports and HDR10+, a direct rival to LG's C5 minus Dolby Vision.
verdict:
The Samsung S90F OLED is the C5's closest rival and often the better deal. It delivers OLED's perfect blacks, refreshes at up to **144 Hz**, has **four HDMI 2.1 ports**, and supports **HDR10, HDR10+ and HLG**. Samsung does not support Dolby Vision, so Dolby Vision streams and discs play in HDR10 instead.

One detail to know: most 55", 65" and 77" sets use Samsung Display's **QD-OLED** panels, prized for vivid color, but some sizes and batches use WOLED panels instead. Both look excellent, but if you want a specific panel type, check reviews for your size. Sizing maths is the same as any 16:9 set: a 65" (56.7" wide) suits seating about **6.5–8.8 ft** away, a 77" (67.1" wide) about **7.7–10.4 ft**. Try our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/) for your room.

In a theater setup, four HDMI 2.1 ports let you connect a receiver or soundbar over eARC and still have three 4K/120-capable inputs. At 144 Hz, each frame lasts about 6.9 ms, good for PC gaming. Brightness is similar to the [LG C5 OLED evo TV](/gear/lg-c5-oled/): fine for dim rooms, less punchy than the [Samsung S95F OLED TV](/gear/samsung-s95f/) in bright ones. If you own a Samsung soundbar, Q-Symphony integration is a bonus; see our [Samsung home theater review](/samsung-home-theater-review/). More picks in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/).

name: Samsung S95F OLED TV
summary: Samsung's flagship QD-OLED with a matte anti-glare screen, 165 Hz and very high brightness, the best OLED for bright rooms.
verdict:
The Samsung S95F OLED is the OLED for rooms that are not dark. Its **QD-OLED** panel uses Samsung's **Glare Free** matte finish, which scatters reflections from windows and lamps instead of mirroring them. Add very high brightness, a **165 Hz** refresh rate, **four HDMI 2.1 ports** and **HDR10+**, and it is one of the most capable TVs available.

Here is why the matte screen matters in a theater that doubles as a living room. On a glossy OLED, a lamp behind your seat shows as a bright spot on dark scenes; on the S95F it becomes a soft haze that is far easier to ignore. Brightness adds to that: a projector at 60 foot-lamberts gives about 205 nits, while flagship OLED HDR highlights run several times higher, so the S95F keeps punch even in daylight. See [HDR explained](/glossary/hdr/).

For sizing, a 65" (56.7" wide) suits seats about **6.5–8.8 ft** back, a 77" (67.1" wide) about 7.7–10.4 ft, and an 83" (72.3" wide) about 8.3–11.2 ft; check our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/). At 165 Hz each frame lasts about 6.1 ms. The trade-offs are price, no Dolby Vision, and a matte finish that can make blacks look a touch lifted under direct light. In a dark room, a glossy LG OLED such as the [LG C6 OLED evo TV](/gear/lg-c6-oled/) is just as good for less. See our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/) and our [Samsung home theater review](/samsung-home-theater-review/).

name: Sony Bravia 8 II OLED TV
summary: A QD-OLED with Sony's excellent processing and natural, accurate color, the film lover's OLED, held back by only two HDMI 2.1 ports.
verdict:
The Sony Bravia 8 II is the OLED for viewers who care most about **picture accuracy and processing**. It uses a **QD-OLED** panel, supports **Dolby Vision, HDR10 and HLG**, runs **Google TV**, and independent reviews praise its motion handling, upscaling and faithful color, which are Sony's strengths. It comes in 55" and 65" only.

The ports need planning in a theater. It has four HDMI inputs, but only **two are HDMI 2.1** with 4K/120, and one of those two is the **eARC** port (see [eARC](/glossary/earc/)). If your soundbar or receiver connects over eARC, that leaves **one** 4K/120 input for a console. With a receiver that has its own HDMI 2.1 inputs, route consoles through the receiver instead; see our [Sony home theater review](/sony-home-theater-review/) for pairing ideas.

Sizing caps out at 65", which is 56.7" wide. That suits seats about **6.5–8.8 ft** away (40 to 30 degrees); beyond about 9 ft, the image will feel small for a theater. Check with our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/). Refresh is 120 Hz rather than 144 Hz, which only matters to PC gamers. If you want a bigger screen, the [LG C5 OLED evo TV](/gear/lg-c5-oled/) and [Samsung S90F OLED TV](/gear/samsung-s90f/) go to 77" and 83"; if you want Sony processing at larger sizes, look at the [Sony Bravia 9 Mini LED TV](/gear/sony-bravia-9/). More in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/).

name: Sony Bravia 9 Mini LED TV
summary: Sony's flagship Mini LED with very high brightness and well-controlled blooming, for big-screen theaters with ambient light.
verdict:
The Sony Bravia 9 is Sony's brightest TV and its answer for big rooms with light. It is a **Mini LED** set with fine-grained local dimming, sold in **65", 75" and 85"**, supporting **Dolby Vision, HDR10 and HLG** on **Google TV**. Independent reviews widely note its very high brightness and how well Sony's processing controls blooming around bright objects.

Bigger sizes change the seating maths. A 75" screen is 65.4" wide, which suits seats about **7.5–10.2 ft** away; an 85" (74.1" wide) about **8.5–11.5 ft**. That is a realistic theater distance where a 65" OLED would feel small. Try our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/). Area grows fast too: an 85" screen has about 70% more area than a 65".

Like the [Sony Bravia 8 II OLED TV](/gear/sony-bravia-8-ii/), it has only **two HDMI 2.1 ports**, one shared with **eARC**, so a soundbar plus two consoles needs planning, or a receiver with its own HDMI 2.1 inputs. Refresh tops out at 120 Hz, and Mini LED will never match OLED's per-pixel blacks, though Sony gets closer than most. Against the cheaper [TCL QM8L SQD-Mini LED TV](/gear/tcl-qm8l/), you pay for processing and refinement rather than raw brightness. For a bright living room theater with long seating distances, it is a top pick in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/).

name: TCL QM8L SQD-Mini LED TV
amazonQuery: TCL 65 inch QM8L SQD-Mini LED TV
summary: TCL's 2026 brightness flagship and the successor to the QM8K: an SQD-Mini LED TV with up to 6,000 nits and 4,000+ dimming zones claimed, 7,000:1 static contrast, 144 Hz and Dolby Vision IQ.
verdict:
The TCL QM8L is the 2026 successor to the QM8K and keeps TCL's brightness-per-dollar lead on paper. TCL calls it **SQD-Mini LED**: up to **4,000+ dimming zones**, up to **6,000 nits** peak, a **7,000:1** static contrast ratio, and an Ultra Color Filter with 5-nanometer particles for purer color. It runs **Google TV with Gemini**, supports **Dolby Vision IQ**, Dolby Atmos and IMAX Enhanced, and has audio by Bang & Olufsen.

The brightness numbers explain why Mini LED wins bright rooms. A projector image at 16 foot-lamberts is about **55 nits** (1 fL is about 3.43 nits), and even a punchy 60 fL is only about 205 nits. A 6,000-nit claim is roughly **30 times** that bright projector for HDR highlights. Sustained real-world brightness will sit below the claim, but this is the class of TV that shrugs off afternoon sun. See [HDR explained](/glossary/hdr/).

For gaming, the panel runs **144 Hz** natively (about 6.9 ms per frame), with Game Accelerator 288 VRR and **AMD FreeSync Premium Pro**. On sizing, the 65" set is about 56.7" wide, which suits seats roughly **6.5–8.8 ft** away; check our [viewing distance calculator](/tools/viewing-distance-calculator/).

The trade-offs are the usual Mini LED ones: some blooming around bright objects on black backgrounds, and some contrast loss off-angle, which TCL's WHVA 2.0 panel aims to reduce. In a dark room, the [LG C6 OLED evo TV](/gear/lg-c6-oled/) still wins on blacks; against the pricier [Sony Bravia 9](/gear/sony-bravia-9/), you give up some processing polish. For a bright living-room theater, it is a top value pick in our [best TV for home theater guide](/best-tv-for-home-theater/).

name: TCL QM7K QD-Mini LED TV
amazonQuery: TCL 65 inch QM7K QD-Mini LED TV
summary: A bright, affordable QD-Mini LED TV with Dolby Vision, HDR10+ and up to 144 Hz, the value pick for big screens.
verdict:
The TCL QM7K brings much of TCL's QM8-series formula down to a lower price. It is a **QD-Mini LED** TV with local dimming, up to **144 Hz**, **Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+, HDR10 and HLG**, and **Google TV**, sold in sizes from 55" up to 98".

The value case is about size. Moving from 65" to 75" adds about 33% more screen area (from about 12.6 to 16.7 sq ft), and with the QM7K that step costs far less than with OLED. Seating maths for a 75" (65.4" wide): about **7.5 ft** for a 40-degree angle and **10.2 ft** for 30 degrees. For an 85" (74.1" wide), about 8.5–11.5 ft. name: Hisense U8QG Mini-LED TV
amazonQuery: Hisense 65 inch U8 Mini-LED TV U8QG
summary: A very bright Mini-LED TV with high refresh, Dolby Vision IQ and HDR10+, a close rival to the TCL QM8L.
verdict:
The Hisense U8QG is Hisense's mainstream flagship Mini-LED TV. It combines high brightness, full-array local dimming, a high-refresh panel of up to **165 Hz**, **Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+, HDR10 and HLG**, and **Google TV**, in sizes from 55" to 100".

The 100" option deserves maths. It is 87.2" wide and covers about 29.7 sq ft, the same as a 100" projector screen, so it suits seats about **10–13.6 ft** away. Unlike a projector, it does not need a dark room or a screen. For a 65" (56.7" wide), aim for about 6.5–8.8 ft; for 75" (65.4" wide), about 7.5–10.2 ft. Brightness is the U8QG's strength, and independent reviews rank it among the brightest Mini LED sets of its generation. faqs.q: Is the Hisense U7SG good for gaming?
faqs.a: Yes. It has a native 165 Hz panel with VRR up to 330 Hz. At 165 Hz each frame lasts about 6.1 ms, which keeps fast games smooth.

faqs.q: Does the Hisense U7SG need a soundbar?
faqs.a: It has a 2.1.2-channel built-in system with Dolby Atmos, which is better than most budget TVs. For a home theater, a soundbar or receiver over HDMI eARC is still the bigger upgrade.
